record.paper_title: On some open problems of number theory
record.original_question: A positive integer is perfect when it is equal to the sum of all of its proper divisors. Is the set of even perfect numbers infinite?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A positive integer $n$ is called perfect if it equals the sum of its proper divisors, equivalently if $\sigma(n) = 2n$, where $\sigma(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} d$ denotes the sum of all positive divisors of $n$. By a classical theorem of Euclid and Euler, an even positive integer $n$ is perfect if and only if $n = 2^{p-1}(2^p - 1)$ for some prime $p$ such that $2^p - 1$ is itself prime (a Mersenne prime).

Determine whether the set of even perfect numbers is infinite. Equivalently, decide whether there exist infinitely many primes $p$ for which $2^p - 1$ is prime.
artifact.status_search_result: The infinitude of even perfect numbers is equivalent to the infinitude of Mersenne primes, a long-standing open problem in number theory. Only a finite number (currently 52) of Mersenne primes are known, and no proof of infinitude exists.

status_evidence.title: Perfect number - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: It is unknown whether there are infinitely many even perfect numbers, which is equivalent to the existence of infinitely many Mersenne primes.
status_evidence.claim: Infinitude of even perfect numbers remains open.

status_evidence.title: Mersenne prime - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: It is conjectured, but unproven, that infinitely many Mersenne primes exist.
status_evidence.claim: Infinitude of Mersenne primes is an open conjecture.
